It is also said: the drink of Paradise has the coldness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a spring therein﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: they will be given to drink from a spring. "Salsabil" is the name of the spring, except that it is declined because it is the end of a verse. In the language it is an attribute of what is in extreme smoothness, so it is as if the spring was described and named by its attribute. I recited to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿named Salsabil﴾, it was said: it is a non-Arabic indefinite noun, and therefore it is declined. It was said: it is a definite noun, but it was made to flow because it is the end of a verse. Mujahid said: "the sharpness of its flow." It was said: "salsabil" means: its water is smooth, pleasant to them. Ibn al-Anbari said: "salsabil" is an attribute of water, for its smoothness and the ease of its passage into the throat. It is said: "sharab salsal," "salsal," and "salsabil." Al-Mawardi related that 'Ali said: the meaning is "sal sabilan ilayha" (ask for a way to it), but this is not sound.

(p-439) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys of everlasting youth﴾ — its explanation has already passed [al-Waqi'ah: 17]. ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾ — meaning in the whiteness and beauty of pearls. Pearls, when scattered from the string over a carpet, look more beautiful than when strung. They were likened to scattered pearls because of their spreading out in service. Had they been in a row, He would have likened them to strung pearls. ﴿And when you look there﴾ — meaning Paradise — ﴿you will see bliss﴾ that cannot be described ﴿and a great dominion﴾ — meaning magnificent, vast; they do not desire anything without being able to attain it, and no angel enters upon them except by permission.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿ʿĀliyahum﴾ — the people of Madinah, Hamzah, and al-Mufaddal from ʿĀsim read it with a sukun on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the hāʾ. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, except that al-Juʿfi from Abu Bakr read "ʿāliyatuhum" with an added ḍammed tāʾ. Anas ibn Malik, Mujahid, and Qatadah read "ʿalayhim" with a fatḥah on the lām and a sukun on the yāʾ, without a tāʾ or an alif.

al-Zajjaj said: As for the grammatical analysis of "ʿāliyihim" with a sukun on the yāʾ, its nominative case is as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and the predicate (khabar) is "thiyabu sundusin" (garments of fine silk). As for "ʿāliyahum" with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, it is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of two things: one of them is from the hāʾ and the mīm, and the meaning is: "there will circulate among the righteous young boys of everlasting youth, bearing (ʿāliyan) for the righteous garments of fine silk," because He described their conditions in Paradise; so the meaning is: "there will circulate over them in this state these ones." It is also permissible that it be a state of the young boys: the meaning is: "when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls in a state of the garments being upon them." As for "ʿāliyatuhum," it has been read with the nominative and the accusative, and these are two good readings in Arabic, except that they contradict the Muṣḥaf, so I do not see reciting them, and their explanation is like the explanation of "ʿāliyahum."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿garments of green fine silk﴾ — Ibn ʿĀmir and Abu ʿAmr read "khuḍrun" in the nominative and "wa-istabraqin" in the genitive. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr from ʿĀsim read "khuḍrin" (p-440) in the genitive and "wa-istabraqun" in the nominative. Nafiʿ and Ḥafs from ʿĀsim read "khuḍrun wa-istabraqun," both in the nominative. Hamzah and al-Kisāʾi read "khuḍarin wa-istabraqin," both in the genitive. al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "khuḍrun" in the nominative, it is an adjective of "thiyab" (garments), and the word "thiyab" is a plural form. Whoever reads "khuḍrin," it is an adjective of "sundus," and "sundus" in meaning refers back to the garments. Whoever reads "wa-istabraqun," it is coordinated with "thiyab"; the meaning is: "upon them is istabraq (brocade)." Whoever reads it in the genitive, he conjoins it with "sundus," so the meaning is: "upon them are garments of these two kinds." We have already explained the meanings of sundus, istabraq, and the bracelets in [al-Kahf: 31].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ — there are two views on this:
One: they do not defecate or urinate from drinking the wine of Paradise; this was said by ʿAtiyyah.
The second: because the wine of Paradise is pure and not impure like the wine of this world; this was said by al-Farraʾ. Abu Qilabah said: After the meal they are brought the pure drink, and they drink, so their bellies become lean through it, and a sweat flows from their skins like the scent of musk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this﴾ — meaning what has been described of the bliss of Paradise — ﴿is a reward for you﴾ in return for your deeds ﴿and your striving has been appreciated﴾ — meaning your work in the world in obedience to Him. ʿAtaʾ said: He means: "I have thanked you for it, and I will reward you with the best of reward." ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in gradual revelation﴾ — meaning We made it detailed in its sending down, so We did not send it down all at once. ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾ — its explanation has already passed in several places [al-Tur: 48; al-Qalam: 48]. The commentators say this is abrogated by the verse of the sword, but this is not sound. ﴿And do not obey from among them one who is sinful or ungrateful﴾ — meaning from among the polytheists of the people of Makkah. "Aw" here is in the sense of "wa" (and), like His saying: ﴿or the entrails﴾ [al-Anʿam: 146]. This has already passed. The commentators have three views regarding the meaning of "the sinful" and "the ungrateful":
(p-441) One: they are two descriptions of Abu Jahl.
The second: the sinful is ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, and the ungrateful is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.
The third: the sinful is al-Walid, and the ungrateful is ʿUtbah; this is because the two of them said to him: "Turn back from this matter, and we will satisfy you with wealth and marriage."

﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾ — meaning: mention Him with monotheism in prayer ﴿in the morning﴾ — meaning the dawn prayer ﴿and in the evening﴾ — meaning the afternoon prayer. Some say: the noon and afternoon prayers. ﴿And during the night prostrate to Him﴾ — meaning the sunset and night prayers. ﴿And glorify Him through the long night﴾ — this is the night prayer; it was obligatory for him, and for his community it is voluntary. ﴿Indeed, these﴾ — meaning the disbelievers of Makkah ﴿love the immediate﴾ — meaning the immediate abode, which is this world ﴿and leave behind them﴾ — meaning before them ﴿a heavy day﴾ — meaning a difficult, severe day. The meaning: they abandon faith in it and working for it. Then He mentioned His power, saying, the Exalted: ﴿We created them and strengthened their joints﴾ — meaning their creation; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Farraʾ, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said: "a woman of good asr," meaning of good form, as if she were bound (usirat), meaning tightened. The origin of this is from al-Isar, which is the rawhide strap with which the saddle-pads are tied. It is said: "How well he tied his saddle-girth," meaning how well he tightened it [with rawhide]. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "their joints." And from al-Hasan who said: "their limbs, some joined to others by the sinews and tendons." ﴿And if We wish, We could replace them with their likes﴾ — meaning: if We wish, We would destroy them and bring others resembling them, making them a substitute in their place. ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ — we have explained this verse in [al-Muzzammil: 19].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you will not, except that Allah wills﴾ — [the attainment of] the way; ﴿except that Allah wills﴾ that for you. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "wa-mā yashāʾūna" with the yāʾ.

(p-442) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ — the commentators said: mercy here is Paradise. ﴿But the wrongdoers﴾ — the polytheists. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the accusative of "al-ẓālimīn" is by proximity (jiwār); the meaning: "and He does not admit the wrongdoers into His mercy." al-Zajjaj said: "al-ẓālimīn" is only in the accusative because there is an accusative before it. The meaning: "He admits whom He wills into His mercy, and punishes the wrongdoers," and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He has prepared for them﴾ is an explanation of this implied element. Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Abu al-Jawzaʾ, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "wa-al-ẓālimūna" in the nominative.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 76, verse 4–31 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Hasan said: they are those who do not harm even an ant. ﴿They drink from a cup﴾, that is, from a vessel containing drink. ﴿Whose mixture is camphor﴾, meaning the mixture of the cup is camphor (kafur). On this there are three opinions.

The second: it is the name of a spring in Paradise, said by 'Ata' and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: the meaning is that its mixture is like camphor for the fineness of its fragrance, permitted by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a spring (ʿaynan)﴾. Al-Farra' said: it explains the camphor. Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative in the sense of "I mean a spring." Al-Zajjaj said: the best view is that the meaning is "from a spring," ﴿from which the servants of Allah drink﴾, and on this there are three opinions.

(p-431) The first: they drink from it. The second: they drink it, and the preposition "bi" is redundant. The third: the servants of Allah drink wine with it, mixing it. Regarding this spring there are two views.

One: it is the camphor previously mentioned.

The second: it is tasnim. "The servants of Allah" here means His friends. ﴿They make it gush forth in abundance﴾. Mujahid said: they lead it wherever they wish in Paradise. Al-Farra' said: wherever a person of Paradise wishes, he makes it gush forth for himself.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They fulfill the vow﴾. Al-Farra' said: there is an implied "kanu" (they used to) fulfill the vow. On this there are two views.

One: they fulfill vows when they vow in obedience to Allah, said by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah.

The second: they fulfill what Allah has obligated upon them, said by Qatadah. The meaning of "nadhr" linguistically is obligation, so the meaning is: they fulfill what is obligatory upon them. ﴿And they fear a Day whose evil is widespread﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: spreading (fashiyan). Ibn Qutaybah said: spreading and dispersing. It is said: "istatar al-hariq" when the fire spreads, and "istatar al-fajr" when the light spreads. They recited for al-A'sha:

(p-432) Muqatil said: its evil was spreading in the heavens, so they split, the stars scattered, the angels were terrified, the sun and the moon were folded up, the mountains were blown away, the waters sank, and everything on the face of the earth was broken, from mountain and building, and the evil of the Day of Resurrection spread throughout it.

One: it was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. He hired himself out to water a palm grove for some barley for a night until morning. When he received the barley, he ground a third of it and prepared some of it for them to eat. When it was ready, a needy person (miskin) came, and they gave it to him. Then he worked on the second third, and when it was finished, an orphan came, and they fed him. Then he worked on the remaining third, and when it was ready, a captive from the polytheists came, and they fed him, and they spent that day fasting. Then these verses were revealed. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah al-Ansari. He fasted a day, and when he wished to break his fast, a needy person, an orphan, and a captive came, and he fed them three loaves, and he had only one loaf left for himself and his family, so this verse was revealed concerning them. This was said by Muqatil.

(p-433) Regarding the pronoun of reference in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿despite their love for it﴾, there are two views.

One: it refers to the food. It is as if they preferred others while they themselves were in need of it. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Zajjaj, and the majority.

The second: it refers to Allah, the Exalted. This was said by al-Darani. The meaning of "miskin and yatim" has already passed under [al-Baqarah: 83]. Regarding the captive (al-asir) there are four views.

One: he is a prisoner from the people of the qibla (Muslims), said by 'Ata', Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr. The second: he is a captive polytheist, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The third: a woman, said by (p-434) Abu Hamzah al-Thumali. The fourth: a slave, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Section
Some exegetes went to the view that the verse includes praise of them for feeding a captive polytheist. They said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword. This view is not worth anything, for in feeding a polytheist captive there is reward, and this is to be understood as voluntary charity. As for the obligatory, it is not permissible to direct it to disbelievers, as mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah﴾, that is, seeking the reward of Allah. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: indeed, they did not say this, but Allah knew it from their hearts, so He praised them for it so that whoever desires this may be encouraged.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We do not want from you reward﴾, that is, in deed, ﴿nor thanks﴾ in words. ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day﴾, that is, a day that is ﴿stern (ʿabusan)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: its faces frown in it, so he made it a description of the day, like His saying: ﴿on a windy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], meaning a windy day of wind. As for "qamtarir," Ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it means long. 'Awfi narrated from him that he said: it is the day in which a man's brow contracts. On this view the day is described by what occurs in it, as we said regarding "stern," since a day is not described as contracting what is between the eyes. Mujahid and Qatadah said: (p-435) "qamtarir" is that which contracts faces, draws in life, and what is between the eyes from its severity. al-Farra' said: it is severe. It is said: a "qamtarir" day, and a "qumatir" day. Someone recited to me:
(O sons of our paternal uncle, do you remember our trial upon you when there is a qumatir day?)
Abu 'Ubaydah said: "'abus," "qamtarir," "qumatir," "'asib," and "'asbasb" are the most intense of days and the longest in calamity.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So Allah protected them from the evil of that day﴾ because of their obedience in the world, ﴿and gave them radiance (nadrah)﴾, that is, beauty and whiteness in the faces, ﴿and joy﴾ that has no end. Al-Hasan said: radiance is in the faces and joy is in the hearts. ﴿And He rewarded them for what they endured﴾ in obeying Him and in refraining from disobeying Him, ﴿with a garden and silk﴾, which is the clothing of the people of Paradise. ﴿Reclining therein﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning He rewarded them with a garden while reclining therein.

We have already explained this under [al-Kahf: 31].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not see therein a sun﴾ whose heat would harm them, ﴿nor extreme cold (zamharir)﴾, which is severe cold. The meaning is that they will find neither heat nor cold therein. It is related from Tha'lab that he said: "al-zamharir" is the moon, and he recited:
(And a night whose darkness has gathered, I crossed it while the zamharir had not shone.)
That is, the moon had not risen.

(p-436) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And near [dāniyatan]﴾. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: and He rewarded them with a garden, ﴿and near to them its shades﴾, that is, the shades of its trees are close to them. ﴿And its fruit-clusters are made fully submissive﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: when one intends to take from its fruits, they lower themselves to him until he takes what he wants. Others said: they are brought near to them made docile however they wish, so they take them standing, sitting, and reclining, like His saying: ﴿its clusters are near [to hand]﴾ [al-Haqqah: 23]. As for "al-akwab" (cups), we have explained them under [al-Zukhruf: 71]. ﴿They are crystal (qawarira)﴾, that is, those cups are crystal, but they are of silver. Ibn 'Abbas said: if you were to beat the silver of this world until it became like the wing of a fly, the water would not be seen behind it, and the crystal of Paradise is of silver with the clarity of crystal. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: this is by way of comparison; the meaning is: as if they were of silver, that is, they have a whiteness like the whiteness of silver and a clarity like the clarity of crystal.

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim used to read "qawarira qawarira," joining both with tanwin and pausing on both with an alif. Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah joined both without tanwin and paused on both without alif. Ibn Kathir joined the first with tanwin and paused on it with an alif, and joined the second without tanwin and paused without alif. Hafs narrated from 'Asim that he read "salasil" and "qawarira qawarira," joining all three without tanwin and pausing on all three with an alif. Abu 'Amr used to read the first "qawarira" and pause on it with an alif, and join without tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said: the preferred view among the grammarians is that "qawarira" is not declined, because every plural that has two letters after its alif is not declined. Whoever read "qawarira" with tanwin declined the first as a sign of the end of a verse, and left the second undeclined because it is not the end of a verse. Whoever declined the second made the wording follow the wording, because the Arabs sometimes change the i'rab (grammatical case-ending) of a thing to make the wording follow the wording, as they said: "juhr dabb kharib" (the hole of a lizard, ruined), whereas "kharib" (ruined) is actually an attribute of "juhr" (hole).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They have measured them with a measure﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu 'Imran, al-Jahdari, and Ibn Ya'mar read "qudirul" with a raised qaf, a kasra on the dal, and its shadda. Humayd and 'Amr ibn Dinar read "qaddarul" with a fatha on the qaf and dal, and without shadda.

Then there are two views on the meaning of the verse.

One: they measured them in their own souls, so they came according to what they measured. This was said by al-Hasan. Al-Zajjaj said: the vessel was made to the measure of what they need and desire, according to their measure.

The second: they measured them to an amount that neither exceeds nor falls short, said by Mujahid. Others said: the cup was measured to the amount of their quenching, not exceeding their quenching so as to weigh down the hand, nor falling short so as to seek more; and this is the most delicious of drinks. On this view the pronoun in "qaddarū" refers to the cupbearers and servants; on the first view it refers to the drinkers.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will be given to drink therein﴾, meaning in Paradise, ﴿a cup whose mixture is ginger (zanjabil)﴾. The Arabs strike the proverb with ginger and wine mixed together. Al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas said, describing the mouth of a woman:
(So the taste of ginger in it is as if, when you tasted it, it were the pure essence of wine.)

(p-438) Another said:
(As if cloves and ginger had spent the night in her mouth, and honey extracted from the hives.)
Al-aryu is honey, and al-mushar is what is extracted from the beehives. Mujahid said: "zanjabil" is the name of the spring from which the drink of the righteous is taken. I recited to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: "zanjabil" is arabized. Al-Dinawari said: it grows in the fertile lands of 'Oman; it is roots that spread through the earth, and it is not a tree eaten fresh; the best of what is carried comes from the lands of China. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that in it is the taste of ginger, and the discussion of it is like the earlier discussion about camphor. It is also said: the drink of Paradise has the coldness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a spring therein﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: they will be given to drink from a spring. "Salsabil" is the name of the spring, except that it is declined because it is the end of a verse. In the language it is an attribute of what is in extreme smoothness, so it is as if the spring was described and named by its attribute. I recited to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿named Salsabil﴾, it was said: it is a non-Arabic indefinite noun, and therefore it is declined. It was said: it is a definite noun, but it was made to flow because it is the end of a verse. Mujahid said: "the sharpness of its flow." It was said: "salsabil" means: its water is smooth, pleasant to them. Ibn al-Anbari said: "salsabil" is an attribute of water, for its smoothness and the ease of its passage into the throat. It is said: "sharab salsal," "salsal," and "salsabil." Al-Mawardi related that 'Ali said: the meaning is "sal sabilan ilayha" (ask for a way to it), but this is not sound.

(p-439) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys of everlasting youth﴾ — its explanation has already passed [al-Waqi'ah: 17]. ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾ — meaning in the whiteness and beauty of pearls. Pearls, when scattered from the string over a carpet, look more beautiful than when strung. They were likened to scattered pearls because of their spreading out in service. Had they been in a row, He would have likened them to strung pearls. ﴿And when you look there﴾ — meaning Paradise — ﴿you will see bliss﴾ that cannot be described ﴿and a great dominion﴾ — meaning magnificent, vast; they do not desire anything without being able to attain it, and no angel enters upon them except by permission.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿ʿĀliyahum﴾ — the people of Madinah, Hamzah, and al-Mufaddal from ʿĀsim read it with a sukun on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the hāʾ. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, except that al-Juʿfi from Abu Bakr read "ʿāliyatuhum" with an added ḍammed tāʾ. Anas ibn Malik, Mujahid, and Qatadah read "ʿalayhim" with a fatḥah on the lām and a sukun on the yāʾ, without a tāʾ or an alif.

al-Zajjaj said: As for the grammatical analysis of "ʿāliyihim" with a sukun on the yāʾ, its nominative case is as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and the predicate (khabar) is "thiyabu sundusin" (garments of fine silk). As for "ʿāliyahum" with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, it is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of two things: one of them is from the hāʾ and the mīm, and the meaning is: "there will circulate among the righteous young boys of everlasting youth, bearing (ʿāliyan) for the righteous garments of fine silk," because He described their conditions in Paradise; so the meaning is: "there will circulate over them in this state these ones." It is also permissible that it be a state of the young boys: the meaning is: "when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls in a state of the garments being upon them." As for "ʿāliyatuhum," it has been read with the nominative and the accusative, and these are two good readings in Arabic, except that they contradict the Muṣḥaf, so I do not see reciting them, and their explanation is like the explanation of "ʿāliyahum."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿garments of green fine silk﴾ — Ibn ʿĀmir and Abu ʿAmr read "khuḍrun" in the nominative and "wa-istabraqin" in the genitive. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr from ʿĀsim read "khuḍrin" (p-440) in the genitive and "wa-istabraqun" in the nominative. Nafiʿ and Ḥafs from ʿĀsim read "khuḍrun wa-istabraqun," both in the nominative. Hamzah and al-Kisāʾi read "khuḍarin wa-istabraqin," both in the genitive. al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "khuḍrun" in the nominative, it is an adjective of "thiyab" (garments), and the word "thiyab" is a plural form. Whoever reads "khuḍrin," it is an adjective of "sundus," and "sundus" in meaning refers back to the garments. Whoever reads "wa-istabraqun," it is coordinated with "thiyab"; the meaning is: "upon them is istabraq (brocade)." Whoever reads it in the genitive, he conjoins it with "sundus," so the meaning is: "upon them are garments of these two kinds." We have already explained the meanings of sundus, istabraq, and the bracelets in [al-Kahf: 31].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ — there are two views on this:
One: they do not defecate or urinate from drinking the wine of Paradise; this was said by ʿAtiyyah.
The second: because the wine of Paradise is pure and not impure like the wine of this world; this was said by al-Farraʾ. Abu Qilabah said: After the meal they are brought the pure drink, and they drink, so their bellies become lean through it, and a sweat flows from their skins like the scent of musk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this﴾ — meaning what has been described of the bliss of Paradise — ﴿is a reward for you﴾ in return for your deeds ﴿and your striving has been appreciated﴾ — meaning your work in the world in obedience to Him. ʿAtaʾ said: He means: "I have thanked you for it, and I will reward you with the best of reward." ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in gradual revelation﴾ — meaning We made it detailed in its sending down, so We did not send it down all at once. ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾ — its explanation has already passed in several places [al-Tur: 48; al-Qalam: 48]. The commentators say this is abrogated by the verse of the sword, but this is not sound. ﴿And do not obey from among them one who is sinful or ungrateful﴾ — meaning from among the polytheists of the people of Makkah. "Aw" here is in the sense of "wa" (and), like His saying: ﴿or the entrails﴾ [al-Anʿam: 146]. This has already passed. The commentators have three views regarding the meaning of "the sinful" and "the ungrateful":
(p-441) One: they are two descriptions of Abu Jahl.
The second: the sinful is ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, and the ungrateful is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.
The third: the sinful is al-Walid, and the ungrateful is ʿUtbah; this is because the two of them said to him: "Turn back from this matter, and we will satisfy you with wealth and marriage."

﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾ — meaning: mention Him with monotheism in prayer ﴿in the morning﴾ — meaning the dawn prayer ﴿and in the evening﴾ — meaning the afternoon prayer. Some say: the noon and afternoon prayers. ﴿And during the night prostrate to Him﴾ — meaning the sunset and night prayers. ﴿And glorify Him through the long night﴾ — this is the night prayer; it was obligatory for him, and for his community it is voluntary. ﴿Indeed, these﴾ — meaning the disbelievers of Makkah ﴿love the immediate﴾ — meaning the immediate abode, which is this world ﴿and leave behind them﴾ — meaning before them ﴿a heavy day﴾ — meaning a difficult, severe day. The meaning: they abandon faith in it and working for it. Then He mentioned His power, saying, the Exalted: ﴿We created them and strengthened their joints﴾ — meaning their creation; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Farraʾ, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said: "a woman of good asr," meaning of good form, as if she were bound (usirat), meaning tightened. The origin of this is from al-Isar, which is the rawhide strap with which the saddle-pads are tied. It is said: "How well he tied his saddle-girth," meaning how well he tightened it [with rawhide]. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "their joints." And from al-Hasan who said: "their limbs, some joined to others by the sinews and tendons." ﴿And if We wish, We could replace them with their likes﴾ — meaning: if We wish, We would destroy them and bring others resembling them, making them a substitute in their place. ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ — we have explained this verse in [al-Muzzammil: 19].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you will not, except that Allah wills﴾ — [the attainment of] the way; ﴿except that Allah wills﴾ that for you. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "wa-mā yashāʾūna" with the yāʾ.

(p-442) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ — the commentators said: mercy here is Paradise. ﴿But the wrongdoers﴾ — the polytheists. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the accusative of "al-ẓālimīn" is by proximity (jiwār); the meaning: "and He does not admit the wrongdoers into His mercy." al-Zajjaj said: "al-ẓālimīn" is only in the accusative because there is an accusative before it. The meaning: "He admits whom He wills into His mercy, and punishes the wrongdoers," and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He has prepared for them﴾ is an explanation of this implied element. Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Abu al-Jawzaʾ, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "wa-al-ẓālimūna" in the nominative.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 76, verse 4–31 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: (Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains [salasil]). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "salasila" without tanwin, and they pause on it with an alif. Abu 'Amr paused on it with an alif. Makki ibn Abi Talib the grammarian said: "salasil" and "qawarir" are originally not declined (ghayr munsarif, diptotes), and whoever of the readers declined it, that is a dialect of some of the Arabs. It was also said: he declined it only because it is written with an alif in the Mushaf, so he declined it to follow the orthography of the Mushaf. Muqatil said: the chains are around their necks, and the shackles (al-aghlal) are on their hands. We have already explained the meaning of "al-sa'ir" under [al-Nisa': 10].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the righteous (al-abrar)﴾. Its singular is barr and barr (bārr), and they are the truthful. It was said: the obedient. Al-Hasan said: they are those who do not harm even an ant. ﴿They drink from a cup﴾, that is, from a vessel containing drink. ﴿Whose mixture is camphor﴾, meaning the mixture of the cup is camphor (kafur). On this there are three opinions.

The first: it is the well-known camphor. This was said by Mujahid and Muqatil. On this view, regarding what is meant by "camphor," there are three opinions: its coldness, said by al-Hasan; its fragrance, said by Qatadah; and its taste, said by al-Suddi.

The second: it is the name of a spring in Paradise, said by 'Ata' and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: the meaning is that its mixture is like camphor for the fineness of its fragrance, permitted by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a spring (ʿaynan)﴾. Al-Farra' said: it explains the camphor. Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative in the sense of "I mean a spring." Al-Zajjaj said: the best view is that the meaning is "from a spring," ﴿from which the servants of Allah drink﴾, and on this there are three opinions.

(p-431) The first: they drink from it. The second: they drink it, and the preposition "bi" is redundant. The third: the servants of Allah drink wine with it, mixing it. Regarding this spring there are two views.

One: it is the camphor previously mentioned.

The second: it is tasnim. "The servants of Allah" here means His friends. ﴿They make it gush forth in abundance﴾. Mujahid said: they lead it wherever they wish in Paradise. Al-Farra' said: wherever a person of Paradise wishes, he makes it gush forth for himself.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They fulfill the vow﴾. Al-Farra' said: there is an implied "kanu" (they used to) fulfill the vow. On this there are two views.

One: they fulfill vows when they vow in obedience to Allah, said by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah.

The second: they fulfill what Allah has obligated upon them, said by Qatadah. The meaning of "nadhr" linguistically is obligation, so the meaning is: they fulfill what is obligatory upon them. ﴿And they fear a Day whose evil is widespread﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: spreading (fashiyan). Ibn Qutaybah said: spreading and dispersing. It is said: "istatar al-hariq" when the fire spreads, and "istatar al-fajr" when the light spreads. They recited for al-A'sha:
(Then she departed, and she had left in the heart a crack, despite her distance, spreading out.)

(p-432) Muqatil said: its evil was spreading in the heavens, so they split, the stars scattered, the angels were terrified, the sun and the moon were folded up, the mountains were blown away, the waters sank, and everything on the face of the earth was broken, from mountain and building, and the evil of the Day of Resurrection spread throughout it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they feed the food despite their love for it﴾. They differed about who it was revealed concerning, on two views.

One: it was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. He hired himself out to water a palm grove for some barley for a night until morning. When he received the barley, he ground a third of it and prepared some of it for them to eat. When it was ready, a needy person (miskin) came, and they gave it to him. Then he worked on the second third, and when it was finished, an orphan came, and they fed him. Then he worked on the remaining third, and when it was ready, a captive from the polytheists came, and they fed him, and they spent that day fasting. Then these verses were revealed. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah al-Ansari. He fasted a day, and when he wished to break his fast, a needy person, an orphan, and a captive came, and he fed them three loaves, and he had only one loaf left for himself and his family, so this verse was revealed concerning them. This was said by Muqatil.

(p-433) Regarding the pronoun of reference in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿despite their love for it﴾, there are two views.

One: it refers to the food. It is as if they preferred others while they themselves were in need of it. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Zajjaj, and the majority.

The second: it refers to Allah, the Exalted. This was said by al-Darani. The meaning of "miskin and yatim" has already passed under [al-Baqarah: 83]. Regarding the captive (al-asir) there are four views.

One: he is a prisoner from the people of the qibla (Muslims), said by 'Ata', Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr. The second: he is a captive polytheist, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The third: a woman, said by (p-434) Abu Hamzah al-Thumali. The fourth: a slave, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Section
Some exegetes went to the view that the verse includes praise of them for feeding a captive polytheist. They said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword. This view is not worth anything, for in feeding a polytheist captive there is reward, and this is to be understood as voluntary charity. As for the obligatory, it is not permissible to direct it to disbelievers, as mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah﴾, that is, seeking the reward of Allah. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: indeed, they did not say this, but Allah knew it from their hearts, so He praised them for it so that whoever desires this may be encouraged.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We do not want from you reward﴾, that is, in deed, ﴿nor thanks﴾ in words. ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day﴾, that is, a day that is ﴿stern (ʿabusan)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: its faces frown in it, so he made it a description of the day, like His saying: ﴿on a windy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], meaning a windy day of wind. As for "qamtarir," Ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it means long. 'Awfi narrated from him that he said: it is the day in which a man's brow contracts. On this view the day is described by what occurs in it, as we said regarding "stern," since a day is not described as contracting what is between the eyes. Mujahid and Qatadah said: (p-435) "qamtarir" is that which contracts faces, draws in life, and what is between the eyes from its severity. al-Farra' said: it is severe. It is said: a "qamtarir" day, and a "qumatir" day. Someone recited to me:
(O sons of our paternal uncle, do you remember our trial upon you when there is a qumatir day?)
Abu 'Ubaydah said: "'abus," "qamtarir," "qumatir," "'asib," and "'asbasb" are the most intense of days and the longest in calamity.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So Allah protected them from the evil of that day﴾ because of their obedience in the world, ﴿and gave them radiance (nadrah)﴾, that is, beauty and whiteness in the faces, ﴿and joy﴾ that has no end. Al-Hasan said: radiance is in the faces and joy is in the hearts. ﴿And He rewarded them for what they endured﴾ in obeying Him and in refraining from disobeying Him, ﴿with a garden and silk﴾, which is the clothing of the people of Paradise. ﴿Reclining therein﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning He rewarded them with a garden while reclining therein.

We have already explained this under [al-Kahf: 31].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not see therein a sun﴾ whose heat would harm them, ﴿nor extreme cold (zamharir)﴾, which is severe cold. The meaning is that they will find neither heat nor cold therein. It is related from Tha'lab that he said: "al-zamharir" is the moon, and he recited:
(And a night whose darkness has gathered, I crossed it while the zamharir had not shone.)
That is, the moon had not risen.

(p-436) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And near [dāniyatan]﴾. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: and He rewarded them with a garden, ﴿and near to them its shades﴾, that is, the shades of its trees are close to them. ﴿And its fruit-clusters are made fully submissive﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: when one intends to take from its fruits, they lower themselves to him until he takes what he wants. Others said: they are brought near to them made docile however they wish, so they take them standing, sitting, and reclining, like His saying: ﴿its clusters are near [to hand]﴾ [al-Haqqah: 23]. As for "al-akwab" (cups), we have explained them under [al-Zukhruf: 71]. ﴿They are crystal (qawarira)﴾, that is, those cups are crystal, but they are of silver. Ibn 'Abbas said: if you were to beat the silver of this world until it became like the wing of a fly, the water would not be seen behind it, and the crystal of Paradise is of silver with the clarity of crystal. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: this is by way of comparison; the meaning is: as if they were of silver, that is, they have a whiteness like the whiteness of silver and a clarity like the clarity of crystal.

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim used to read "qawarira qawarira," joining both with tanwin and pausing on both with an alif. Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah joined both without tanwin and paused on both without alif. Ibn Kathir joined the first with tanwin and paused on it with an alif, and joined the second without tanwin and paused without alif. Hafs narrated from 'Asim that he read "salasil" and "qawarira qawarira," joining all three without tanwin and pausing on all three with an alif. Abu 'Amr used to read the first "qawarira" and pause on it with an alif, and join without tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said: the preferred view among the grammarians is that "qawarira" is not declined, because every plural that has two letters after its alif is not declined. Whoever read "qawarira" with tanwin declined the first as a sign of the end of a verse, and left the second undeclined because it is not the end of a verse. Whoever declined the second made the wording follow the wording, because the Arabs sometimes change the i'rab (grammatical case-ending) of a thing to make the wording follow the wording, as they said: "juhr dabb kharib" (the hole of a lizard, ruined), whereas "kharib" (ruined) is actually an attribute of "juhr" (hole).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They have measured them with a measure﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu 'Imran, al-Jahdari, and Ibn Ya'mar read "qudirul" with a raised qaf, a kasra on the dal, and its shadda. Humayd and 'Amr ibn Dinar read "qaddarul" with a fatha on the qaf and dal, and without shadda.

Then there are two views on the meaning of the verse.

One: they measured them in their own souls, so they came according to what they measured. This was said by al-Hasan. Al-Zajjaj said: the vessel was made to the measure of what they need and desire, according to their measure.

The second: they measured them to an amount that neither exceeds nor falls short, said by Mujahid. Others said: the cup was measured to the amount of their quenching, not exceeding their quenching so as to weigh down the hand, nor falling short so as to seek more; and this is the most delicious of drinks. On this view the pronoun in "qaddarū" refers to the cupbearers and servants; on the first view it refers to the drinkers.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will be given to drink therein﴾, meaning in Paradise, ﴿a cup whose mixture is ginger (zanjabil)﴾. The Arabs strike the proverb with ginger and wine mixed together. Al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas said, describing the mouth of a woman:
(So the taste of ginger in it is as if, when you tasted it, it were the pure essence of wine.)

(p-438) Another said:
(As if cloves and ginger had spent the night in her mouth, and honey extracted from the hives.)
Al-aryu is honey, and al-mushar is what is extracted from the beehives. Mujahid said: "zanjabil" is the name of the spring from which the drink of the righteous is taken. I recited to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: "zanjabil" is arabized. Al-Dinawari said: it grows in the fertile lands of 'Oman; it is roots that spread through the earth, and it is not a tree eaten fresh; the best of what is carried comes from the lands of China. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that in it is the taste of ginger, and the discussion of it is like the earlier discussion about camphor. It is also said: the drink of Paradise has the coldness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a spring therein﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: they will be given to drink from a spring. "Salsabil" is the name of the spring, except that it is declined because it is the end of a verse. In the language it is an attribute of what is in extreme smoothness, so it is as if the spring was described and named by its attribute. I recited to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿named Salsabil﴾, it was said: it is a non-Arabic indefinite noun, and therefore it is declined. It was said: it is a definite noun, but it was made to flow because it is the end of a verse. Mujahid said: "the sharpness of its flow." It was said: "salsabil" means: its water is smooth, pleasant to them. Ibn al-Anbari said: "salsabil" is an attribute of water, for its smoothness and the ease of its passage into the throat. It is said: "sharab salsal," "salsal," and "salsabil." Al-Mawardi related that 'Ali said: the meaning is "sal sabilan ilayha" (ask for a way to it), but this is not sound.

(p-439) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys of everlasting youth﴾ — its explanation has already passed [al-Waqi'ah: 17]. ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾ — meaning in the whiteness and beauty of pearls. Pearls, when scattered from the string over a carpet, look more beautiful than when strung. They were likened to scattered pearls because of their spreading out in service. Had they been in a row, He would have likened them to strung pearls. ﴿And when you look there﴾ — meaning Paradise — ﴿you will see bliss﴾ that cannot be described ﴿and a great dominion﴾ — meaning magnificent, vast; they do not desire anything without being able to attain it, and no angel enters upon them except by permission.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿ʿĀliyahum﴾ — the people of Madinah, Hamzah, and al-Mufaddal from ʿĀsim read it with a sukun on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the hāʾ. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, except that al-Juʿfi from Abu Bakr read "ʿāliyatuhum" with an added ḍammed tāʾ. Anas ibn Malik, Mujahid, and Qatadah read "ʿalayhim" with a fatḥah on the lām and a sukun on the yāʾ, without a tāʾ or an alif.

al-Zajjaj said: As for the grammatical analysis of "ʿāliyihim" with a sukun on the yāʾ, its nominative case is as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and the predicate (khabar) is "thiyabu sundusin" (garments of fine silk). As for "ʿāliyahum" with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, it is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of two things: one of them is from the hāʾ and the mīm, and the meaning is: "there will circulate among the righteous young boys of everlasting youth, bearing (ʿāliyan) for the righteous garments of fine silk," because He described their conditions in Paradise; so the meaning is: "there will circulate over them in this state these ones." It is also permissible that it be a state of the young boys: the meaning is: "when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls in a state of the garments being upon them." As for "ʿāliyatuhum," it has been read with the nominative and the accusative, and these are two good readings in Arabic, except that they contradict the Muṣḥaf, so I do not see reciting them, and their explanation is like the explanation of "ʿāliyahum."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿garments of green fine silk﴾ — Ibn ʿĀmir and Abu ʿAmr read "khuḍrun" in the nominative and "wa-istabraqin" in the genitive. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr from ʿĀsim read "khuḍrin" (p-440) in the genitive and "wa-istabraqun" in the nominative. Nafiʿ and Ḥafs from ʿĀsim read "khuḍrun wa-istabraqun," both in the nominative. Hamzah and al-Kisāʾi read "khuḍarin wa-istabraqin," both in the genitive. al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "khuḍrun" in the nominative, it is an adjective of "thiyab" (garments), and the word "thiyab" is a plural form. Whoever reads "khuḍrin," it is an adjective of "sundus," and "sundus" in meaning refers back to the garments. Whoever reads "wa-istabraqun," it is coordinated with "thiyab"; the meaning is: "upon them is istabraq (brocade)." Whoever reads it in the genitive, he conjoins it with "sundus," so the meaning is: "upon them are garments of these two kinds." We have already explained the meanings of sundus, istabraq, and the bracelets in [al-Kahf: 31].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ — there are two views on this:
One: they do not defecate or urinate from drinking the wine of Paradise; this was said by ʿAtiyyah.
The second: because the wine of Paradise is pure and not impure like the wine of this world; this was said by al-Farraʾ. Abu Qilabah said: After the meal they are brought the pure drink, and they drink, so their bellies become lean through it, and a sweat flows from their skins like the scent of musk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this﴾ — meaning what has been described of the bliss of Paradise — ﴿is a reward for you﴾ in return for your deeds ﴿and your striving has been appreciated﴾ — meaning your work in the world in obedience to Him. ʿAtaʾ said: He means: "I have thanked you for it, and I will reward you with the best of reward." ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in gradual revelation﴾ — meaning We made it detailed in its sending down, so We did not send it down all at once. ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾ — its explanation has already passed in several places [al-Tur: 48; al-Qalam: 48]. The commentators say this is abrogated by the verse of the sword, but this is not sound. ﴿And do not obey from among them one who is sinful or ungrateful﴾ — meaning from among the polytheists of the people of Makkah. "Aw" here is in the sense of "wa" (and), like His saying: ﴿or the entrails﴾ [al-Anʿam: 146]. This has already passed. The commentators have three views regarding the meaning of "the sinful" and "the ungrateful":
(p-441) One: they are two descriptions of Abu Jahl.
The second: the sinful is ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, and the ungrateful is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.
The third: the sinful is al-Walid, and the ungrateful is ʿUtbah; this is because the two of them said to him: "Turn back from this matter, and we will satisfy you with wealth and marriage."

﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾ — meaning: mention Him with monotheism in prayer ﴿in the morning﴾ — meaning the dawn prayer ﴿and in the evening﴾ — meaning the afternoon prayer. Some say: the noon and afternoon prayers. ﴿And during the night prostrate to Him﴾ — meaning the sunset and night prayers. ﴿And glorify Him through the long night﴾ — this is the night prayer; it was obligatory for him, and for his community it is voluntary. ﴿Indeed, these﴾ — meaning the disbelievers of Makkah ﴿love the immediate﴾ — meaning the immediate abode, which is this world ﴿and leave behind them﴾ — meaning before them ﴿a heavy day﴾ — meaning a difficult, severe day. The meaning: they abandon faith in it and working for it. Then He mentioned His power, saying, the Exalted: ﴿We created them and strengthened their joints﴾ — meaning their creation; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Farraʾ, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said: "a woman of good asr," meaning of good form, as if she were bound (usirat), meaning tightened. The origin of this is from al-Isar, which is the rawhide strap with which the saddle-pads are tied. It is said: "How well he tied his saddle-girth," meaning how well he tightened it [with rawhide]. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "their joints." And from al-Hasan who said: "their limbs, some joined to others by the sinews and tendons." ﴿And if We wish, We could replace them with their likes﴾ — meaning: if We wish, We would destroy them and bring others resembling them, making them a substitute in their place. ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ — we have explained this verse in [al-Muzzammil: 19].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you will not, except that Allah wills﴾ — [the attainment of] the way; ﴿except that Allah wills﴾ that for you. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "wa-mā yashāʾūna" with the yāʾ.

(p-442) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ — the commentators said: mercy here is Paradise. ﴿But the wrongdoers﴾ — the polytheists. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the accusative of "al-ẓālimīn" is by proximity (jiwār); the meaning: "and He does not admit the wrongdoers into His mercy." al-Zajjaj said: "al-ẓālimīn" is only in the accusative because there is an accusative before it. The meaning: "He admits whom He wills into His mercy, and punishes the wrongdoers," and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He has prepared for them﴾ is an explanation of this implied element. Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Abu al-Jawzaʾ, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "wa-al-ẓālimūna" in the nominative.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 76, verse 4–31 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: (Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains [salasil]). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "salasila" without tanwin, and they pause on it with an alif. Abu 'Amr paused on it with an alif. Makki ibn Abi Talib the grammarian said: "salasil" and "qawarir" are originally not declined (ghayr munsarif, diptotes), and whoever of the readers declined it, that is a dialect of some of the Arabs. It was also said: he declined it only because it is written with an alif in the Mushaf, so he declined it to follow the orthography of the Mushaf. Muqatil said: the chains are around their necks, and the shackles (al-aghlal) are on their hands. We have already explained the meaning of "al-sa'ir" under [al-Nisa': 10].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the righteous (al-abrar)﴾. Its singular is barr and barr (bārr), and they are the truthful. It was said: the obedient. Al-Hasan said: they are those who do not harm even an ant. ﴿They drink from a cup﴾, that is, from a vessel containing drink. ﴿Whose mixture is camphor﴾, meaning the mixture of the cup is camphor (kafur). On this there are three opinions.

The first: it is the well-known camphor. This was said by Mujahid and Muqatil. On this view, regarding what is meant by "camphor," there are three opinions: its coldness, said by al-Hasan; its fragrance, said by Qatadah; and its taste, said by al-Suddi.

The second: it is the name of a spring in Paradise, said by 'Ata' and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: the meaning is that its mixture is like camphor for the fineness of its fragrance, permitted by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a spring (ʿaynan)﴾. Al-Farra' said: it explains the camphor. Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative in the sense of "I mean a spring." Al-Zajjaj said: the best view is that the meaning is "from a spring," ﴿from which the servants of Allah drink﴾, and on this there are three opinions.

(p-431) The first: they drink from it. The second: they drink it, and the preposition "bi" is redundant. The third: the servants of Allah drink wine with it, mixing it. Regarding this spring there are two views.

One: it is the camphor previously mentioned.

The second: it is tasnim. "The servants of Allah" here means His friends. ﴿They make it gush forth in abundance﴾. Mujahid said: they lead it wherever they wish in Paradise. Al-Farra' said: wherever a person of Paradise wishes, he makes it gush forth for himself.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They fulfill the vow﴾. Al-Farra' said: there is an implied "kanu" (they used to) fulfill the vow. On this there are two views.

One: they fulfill vows when they vow in obedience to Allah, said by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah.

The second: they fulfill what Allah has obligated upon them, said by Qatadah. The meaning of "nadhr" linguistically is obligation, so the meaning is: they fulfill what is obligatory upon them. ﴿And they fear a Day whose evil is widespread﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: spreading (fashiyan). Ibn Qutaybah said: spreading and dispersing. It is said: "istatar al-hariq" when the fire spreads, and "istatar al-fajr" when the light spreads. They recited for al-A'sha:
(Then she departed, and she had left in the heart a crack, despite her distance, spreading out.)

(p-432) Muqatil said: its evil was spreading in the heavens, so they split, the stars scattered, the angels were terrified, the sun and the moon were folded up, the mountains were blown away, the waters sank, and everything on the face of the earth was broken, from mountain and building, and the evil of the Day of Resurrection spread throughout it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they feed the food despite their love for it﴾. They differed about who it was revealed concerning, on two views.

One: it was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. He hired himself out to water a palm grove for some barley for a night until morning. When he received the barley, he ground a third of it and prepared some of it for them to eat. When it was ready, a needy person (miskin) came, and they gave it to him. Then he worked on the second third, and when it was finished, an orphan came, and they fed him. Then he worked on the remaining third, and when it was ready, a captive from the polytheists came, and they fed him, and they spent that day fasting. Then these verses were revealed. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah al-Ansari. He fasted a day, and when he wished to break his fast, a needy person, an orphan, and a captive came, and he fed them three loaves, and he had only one loaf left for himself and his family, so this verse was revealed concerning them. This was said by Muqatil.

(p-433) Regarding the pronoun of reference in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿despite their love for it﴾, there are two views.

One: it refers to the food. It is as if they preferred others while they themselves were in need of it. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Zajjaj, and the majority.

The second: it refers to Allah, the Exalted. This was said by al-Darani. The meaning of "miskin and yatim" has already passed under [al-Baqarah: 83]. Regarding the captive (al-asir) there are four views.

One: he is a prisoner from the people of the qibla (Muslims), said by 'Ata', Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr. The second: he is a captive polytheist, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The third: a woman, said by (p-434) Abu Hamzah al-Thumali. The fourth: a slave, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Section
Some exegetes went to the view that the verse includes praise of them for feeding a captive polytheist. They said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword. This view is not worth anything, for in feeding a polytheist captive there is reward, and this is to be understood as voluntary charity. As for the obligatory, it is not permissible to direct it to disbelievers, as mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah﴾, that is, seeking the reward of Allah. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: indeed, they did not say this, but Allah knew it from their hearts, so He praised them for it so that whoever desires this may be encouraged.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We do not want from you reward﴾, that is, in deed, ﴿nor thanks﴾ in words. ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day﴾, that is, a day that is ﴿stern (ʿabusan)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: its faces frown in it, so he made it a description of the day, like His saying: ﴿on a windy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], meaning a windy day of wind. As for "qamtarir," Ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it means long. 'Awfi narrated from him that he said: it is the day in which a man's brow contracts. On this view the day is described by what occurs in it, as we said regarding "stern," since a day is not described as contracting what is between the eyes. Mujahid and Qatadah said: (p-435) "qamtarir" is that which contracts faces, draws in life, and what is between the eyes from its severity. al-Farra' said: it is severe. It is said: a "qamtarir" day, and a "qumatir" day. Someone recited to me:
(O sons of our paternal uncle, do you remember our trial upon you when there is a qumatir day?)
Abu 'Ubaydah said: "'abus," "qamtarir," "qumatir," "'asib," and "'asbasb" are the most intense of days and the longest in calamity.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So Allah protected them from the evil of that day﴾ because of their obedience in the world, ﴿and gave them radiance (nadrah)﴾, that is, beauty and whiteness in the faces, ﴿and joy﴾ that has no end. Al-Hasan said: radiance is in the faces and joy is in the hearts. ﴿And He rewarded them for what they endured﴾ in obeying Him and in refraining from disobeying Him, ﴿with a garden and silk﴾, which is the clothing of the people of Paradise. ﴿Reclining therein﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning He rewarded them with a garden while reclining therein.

We have already explained this under [al-Kahf: 31].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not see therein a sun﴾ whose heat would harm them, ﴿nor extreme cold (zamharir)﴾, which is severe cold. The meaning is that they will find neither heat nor cold therein. It is related from Tha'lab that he said: "al-zamharir" is the moon, and he recited:
(And a night whose darkness has gathered, I crossed it while the zamharir had not shone.)
That is, the moon had not risen.

(p-436) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And near [dāniyatan]﴾. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: and He rewarded them with a garden, ﴿and near to them its shades﴾, that is, the shades of its trees are close to them. ﴿And its fruit-clusters are made fully submissive﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: when one intends to take from its fruits, they lower themselves to him until he takes what he wants. Others said: they are brought near to them made docile however they wish, so they take them standing, sitting, and reclining, like His saying: ﴿its clusters are near [to hand]﴾ [al-Haqqah: 23]. As for "al-akwab" (cups), we have explained them under [al-Zukhruf: 71]. ﴿They are crystal (qawarira)﴾, that is, those cups are crystal, but they are of silver. Ibn 'Abbas said: if you were to beat the silver of this world until it became like the wing of a fly, the water would not be seen behind it, and the crystal of Paradise is of silver with the clarity of crystal. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: this is by way of comparison; the meaning is: as if they were of silver, that is, they have a whiteness like the whiteness of silver and a clarity like the clarity of crystal.

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim used to read "qawarira qawarira," joining both with tanwin and pausing on both with an alif. Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah joined both without tanwin and paused on both without alif. Ibn Kathir joined the first with tanwin and paused on it with an alif, and joined the second without tanwin and paused without alif. Hafs narrated from 'Asim that he read "salasil" and "qawarira qawarira," joining all three without tanwin and pausing on all three with an alif. Abu 'Amr used to read the first "qawarira" and pause on it with an alif, and join without tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said: the preferred view among the grammarians is that "qawarira" is not declined, because every plural that has two letters after its alif is not declined. Whoever read "qawarira" with tanwin declined the first as a sign of the end of a verse, and left the second undeclined because it is not the end of a verse. Whoever declined the second made the wording follow the wording, because the Arabs sometimes change the i'rab (grammatical case-ending) of a thing to make the wording follow the wording, as they said: "juhr dabb kharib" (the hole of a lizard, ruined), whereas "kharib" (ruined) is actually an attribute of "juhr" (hole).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They have measured them with a measure﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu 'Imran, al-Jahdari, and Ibn Ya'mar read "qudirul" with a raised qaf, a kasra on the dal, and its shadda. Humayd and 'Amr ibn Dinar read "qaddarul" with a fatha on the qaf and dal, and without shadda.

Then there are two views on the meaning of the verse.

One: they measured them in their own souls, so they came according to what they measured. This was said by al-Hasan. Al-Zajjaj said: the vessel was made to the measure of what they need and desire, according to their measure.

The second: they measured them to an amount that neither exceeds nor falls short, said by Mujahid. Others said: the cup was measured to the amount of their quenching, not exceeding their quenching so as to weigh down the hand, nor falling short so as to seek more; and this is the most delicious of drinks. On this view the pronoun in "qaddarū" refers to the cupbearers and servants; on the first view it refers to the drinkers.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will be given to drink therein﴾, meaning in Paradise, ﴿a cup whose mixture is ginger (zanjabil)﴾. The Arabs strike the proverb with ginger and wine mixed together. Al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas said, describing the mouth of a woman:
(So the taste of ginger in it is as if, when you tasted it, it were the pure essence of wine.)

(p-438) Another said:
(As if cloves and ginger had spent the night in her mouth, and honey extracted from the hives.)
Al-aryu is honey, and al-mushar is what is extracted from the beehives. Mujahid said: "zanjabil" is the name of the spring from which the drink of the righteous is taken. I recited to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: "zanjabil" is arabized. Al-Dinawari said: it grows in the fertile lands of 'Oman; it is roots that spread through the earth, and it is not a tree eaten fresh; the best of what is carried comes from the lands of China. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that in it is the taste of ginger, and the discussion of it is like the earlier discussion about camphor. It is also said: the drink of Paradise has the coldness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a spring therein﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: they will be given to drink from a spring. "Salsabil" is the name of the spring, except that it is declined because it is the end of a verse. In the language it is an attribute of what is in extreme smoothness, so it is as if the spring was described and named by its attribute. I recited to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿named Salsabil﴾, it was said: it is a non-Arabic indefinite noun, and therefore it is declined. It was said: it is a definite noun, but it was made to flow because it is the end of a verse. Mujahid said: "the sharpness of its flow." It was said: "salsabil" means: its water is smooth, pleasant to them. Ibn al-Anbari said: "salsabil" is an attribute of water, for its smoothness and the ease of its passage into the throat. It is said: "sharab salsal," "salsal," and "salsabil." Al-Mawardi related that 'Ali said: the meaning is "sal sabilan ilayha" (ask for a way to it), but this is not sound.

(p-439) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys of everlasting youth﴾ — its explanation has already passed [al-Waqi'ah: 17]. ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾ — meaning in the whiteness and beauty of pearls. Pearls, when scattered from the string over a carpet, look more beautiful than when strung. They were likened to scattered pearls because of their spreading out in service. Had they been in a row, He would have likened them to strung pearls. ﴿And when you look there﴾ — meaning Paradise — ﴿you will see bliss﴾ that cannot be described ﴿and a great dominion﴾ — meaning magnificent, vast; they do not desire anything without being able to attain it, and no angel enters upon them except by permission.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿ʿĀliyahum﴾ — the people of Madinah, Hamzah, and al-Mufaddal from ʿĀsim read it with a sukun on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the hāʾ. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, except that al-Juʿfi from Abu Bakr read "ʿāliyatuhum" with an added ḍammed tāʾ. Anas ibn Malik, Mujahid, and Qatadah read "ʿalayhim" with a fatḥah on the lām and a sukun on the yāʾ, without a tāʾ or an alif.

al-Zajjaj said: As for the grammatical analysis of "ʿāliyihim" with a sukun on the yāʾ, its nominative case is as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and the predicate (khabar) is "thiyabu sundusin" (garments of fine silk). As for "ʿāliyahum" with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, it is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of two things: one of them is from the hāʾ and the mīm, and the meaning is: "there will circulate among the righteous young boys of everlasting youth, bearing (ʿāliyan) for the righteous garments of fine silk," because He described their conditions in Paradise; so the meaning is: "there will circulate over them in this state these ones." It is also permissible that it be a state of the young boys: the meaning is: "when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls in a state of the garments being upon them." As for "ʿāliyatuhum," it has been read with the nominative and the accusative, and these are two good readings in Arabic, except that they contradict the Muṣḥaf, so I do not see reciting them, and their explanation is like the explanation of "ʿāliyahum."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿garments of green fine silk﴾ — Ibn ʿĀmir and Abu ʿAmr read "khuḍrun" in the nominative and "wa-istabraqin" in the genitive. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr from ʿĀsim read "khuḍrin" (p-440) in the genitive and "wa-istabraqun" in the nominative. Nafiʿ and Ḥafs from ʿĀsim read "khuḍrun wa-istabraqun," both in the nominative. Hamzah and al-Kisāʾi read "khuḍarin wa-istabraqin," both in the genitive. al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "khuḍrun" in the nominative, it is an adjective of "thiyab" (garments), and the word "thiyab" is a plural form. Whoever reads "khuḍrin," it is an adjective of "sundus," and "sundus" in meaning refers back to the garments. Whoever reads "wa-istabraqun," it is coordinated with "thiyab"; the meaning is: "upon them is istabraq (brocade)." Whoever reads it in the genitive, he conjoins it with "sundus," so the meaning is: "upon them are garments of these two kinds." We have already explained the meanings of sundus, istabraq, and the bracelets in [al-Kahf: 31].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ — there are two views on this:
One: they do not defecate or urinate from drinking the wine of Paradise; this was said by ʿAtiyyah.
The second: because the wine of Paradise is pure and not impure like the wine of this world; this was said by al-Farraʾ. Abu Qilabah said: After the meal they are brought the pure drink, and they drink, so their bellies become lean through it, and a sweat flows from their skins like the scent of musk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this﴾ — meaning what has been described of the bliss of Paradise — ﴿is a reward for you﴾ in return for your deeds ﴿and your striving has been appreciated﴾ — meaning your work in the world in obedience to Him. ʿAtaʾ said: He means: "I have thanked you for it, and I will reward you with the best of reward." ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in gradual revelation﴾ — meaning We made it detailed in its sending down, so We did not send it down all at once. ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾ — its explanation has already passed in several places [al-Tur: 48; al-Qalam: 48]. The commentators say this is abrogated by the verse of the sword, but this is not sound. ﴿And do not obey from among them one who is sinful or ungrateful﴾ — meaning from among the polytheists of the people of Makkah. "Aw" here is in the sense of "wa" (and), like His saying: ﴿or the entrails﴾ [al-Anʿam: 146]. This has already passed. The commentators have three views regarding the meaning of "the sinful" and "the ungrateful":
(p-441) One: they are two descriptions of Abu Jahl.
The second: the sinful is ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, and the ungrateful is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.
The third: the sinful is al-Walid, and the ungrateful is ʿUtbah; this is because the two of them said to him: "Turn back from this matter, and we will satisfy you with wealth and marriage."

﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾ — meaning: mention Him with monotheism in prayer ﴿in the morning﴾ — meaning the dawn prayer ﴿and in the evening﴾ — meaning the afternoon prayer. Some say: the noon and afternoon prayers. ﴿And during the night prostrate to Him﴾ — meaning the sunset and night prayers. ﴿And glorify Him through the long night﴾ — this is the night prayer; it was obligatory for him, and for his community it is voluntary. ﴿Indeed, these﴾ — meaning the disbelievers of Makkah ﴿love the immediate﴾ — meaning the immediate abode, which is this world ﴿and leave behind them﴾ — meaning before them ﴿a heavy day﴾ — meaning a difficult, severe day. The meaning: they abandon faith in it and working for it. Then He mentioned His power, saying, the Exalted: ﴿We created them and strengthened their joints﴾ — meaning their creation; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Farraʾ, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said: "a woman of good asr," meaning of good form, as if she were bound (usirat), meaning tightened. The origin of this is from al-Isar, which is the rawhide strap with which the saddle-pads are tied. It is said: "How well he tied his saddle-girth," meaning how well he tightened it [with rawhide]. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "their joints." And from al-Hasan who said: "their limbs, some joined to others by the sinews and tendons." ﴿And if We wish, We could replace them with their likes﴾ — meaning: if We wish, We would destroy them and bring others resembling them, making them a substitute in their place. ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ — we have explained this verse in [al-Muzzammil: 19].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you will not, except that Allah wills﴾ — [the attainment of] the way; ﴿except that Allah wills﴾ that for you. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "wa-mā yashāʾūna" with the yāʾ.

(p-442) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ — the commentators said: mercy here is Paradise. ﴿But the wrongdoers﴾ — the polytheists. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the accusative of "al-ẓālimīn" is by proximity (jiwār); the meaning: "and He does not admit the wrongdoers into His mercy." al-Zajjaj said: "al-ẓālimīn" is only in the accusative because there is an accusative before it. The meaning: "He admits whom He wills into His mercy, and punishes the wrongdoers," and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He has prepared for them﴾ is an explanation of this implied element. Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Abu al-Jawzaʾ, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "wa-al-ẓālimūna" in the nominative.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 76, verse 4–31 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: (Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains [salasil]). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "salasila" without tanwin, and they pause on it with an alif. Abu 'Amr paused on it with an alif. Makki ibn Abi Talib the grammarian said: "salasil" and "qawarir" are originally not declined (ghayr munsarif, diptotes), and whoever of the readers declined it, that is a dialect of some of the Arabs. It was also said: he declined it only because it is written with an alif in the Mushaf, so he declined it to follow the orthography of the Mushaf. Muqatil said: the chains are around their necks, and the shackles (al-aghlal) are on their hands. We have already explained the meaning of "al-sa'ir" under [al-Nisa': 10].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the righteous (al-abrar)﴾. Its singular is barr and barr (bārr), and they are the truthful. It was said: the obedient. Al-Hasan said: they are those who do not harm even an ant. ﴿They drink from a cup﴾, that is, from a vessel containing drink. ﴿Whose mixture is camphor﴾, meaning the mixture of the cup is camphor (kafur). On this there are three opinions.

The first: it is the well-known camphor. This was said by Mujahid and Muqatil. On this view, regarding what is meant by "camphor," there are three opinions: its coldness, said by al-Hasan; its fragrance, said by Qatadah; and its taste, said by al-Suddi.

The second: it is the name of a spring in Paradise, said by 'Ata' and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: the meaning is that its mixture is like camphor for the fineness of its fragrance, permitted by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a spring (ʿaynan)﴾. Al-Farra' said: it explains the camphor. Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative in the sense of "I mean a spring." Al-Zajjaj said: the best view is that the meaning is "from a spring," ﴿from which the servants of Allah drink﴾, and on this there are three opinions.

(p-431) The first: they drink from it. The second: they drink it, and the preposition "bi" is redundant. The third: the servants of Allah drink wine with it, mixing it. Regarding this spring there are two views.

One: it is the camphor previously mentioned.

The second: it is tasnim. "The servants of Allah" here means His friends. ﴿They make it gush forth in abundance﴾. Mujahid said: they lead it wherever they wish in Paradise. Al-Farra' said: wherever a person of Paradise wishes, he makes it gush forth for himself.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They fulfill the vow﴾. Al-Farra' said: there is an implied "kanu" (they used to) fulfill the vow. On this there are two views.

One: they fulfill vows when they vow in obedience to Allah, said by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah.

The second: they fulfill what Allah has obligated upon them, said by Qatadah. The meaning of "nadhr" linguistically is obligation, so the meaning is: they fulfill what is obligatory upon them. ﴿And they fear a Day whose evil is widespread﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: spreading (fashiyan). Ibn Qutaybah said: spreading and dispersing. It is said: "istatar al-hariq" when the fire spreads, and "istatar al-fajr" when the light spreads. They recited for al-A'sha:
(Then she departed, and she had left in the heart a crack, despite her distance, spreading out.)

(p-432) Muqatil said: its evil was spreading in the heavens, so they split, the stars scattered, the angels were terrified, the sun and the moon were folded up, the mountains were blown away, the waters sank, and everything on the face of the earth was broken, from mountain and building, and the evil of the Day of Resurrection spread throughout it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they feed the food despite their love for it﴾. They differed about who it was revealed concerning, on two views.

One: it was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. He hired himself out to water a palm grove for some barley for a night until morning. When he received the barley, he ground a third of it and prepared some of it for them to eat. When it was ready, a needy person (miskin) came, and they gave it to him. Then he worked on the second third, and when it was finished, an orphan came, and they fed him. Then he worked on the remaining third, and when it was ready, a captive from the polytheists came, and they fed him, and they spent that day fasting. Then these verses were revealed. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah al-Ansari. He fasted a day, and when he wished to break his fast, a needy person, an orphan, and a captive came, and he fed them three loaves, and he had only one loaf left for himself and his family, so this verse was revealed concerning them. This was said by Muqatil.

(p-433) Regarding the pronoun of reference in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿despite their love for it﴾, there are two views.

One: it refers to the food. It is as if they preferred others while they themselves were in need of it. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Zajjaj, and the majority.

The second: it refers to Allah, the Exalted. This was said by al-Darani. The meaning of "miskin and yatim" has already passed under [al-Baqarah: 83]. Regarding the captive (al-asir) there are four views.

One: he is a prisoner from the people of the qibla (Muslims), said by 'Ata', Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr. The second: he is a captive polytheist, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The third: a woman, said by (p-434) Abu Hamzah al-Thumali. The fourth: a slave, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Section
Some exegetes went to the view that the verse includes praise of them for feeding a captive polytheist. They said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword. This view is not worth anything, for in feeding a polytheist captive there is reward, and this is to be understood as voluntary charity. As for the obligatory, it is not permissible to direct it to disbelievers, as mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah﴾, that is, seeking the reward of Allah. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: indeed, they did not say this, but Allah knew it from their hearts, so He praised them for it so that whoever desires this may be encouraged.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We do not want from you reward﴾, that is, in deed, ﴿nor thanks﴾ in words. ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day﴾, that is, a day that is ﴿stern (ʿabusan)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: its faces frown in it, so he made it a description of the day, like His saying: ﴿on a windy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], meaning a windy day of wind. As for "qamtarir," Ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it means long. 'Awfi narrated from him that he said: it is the day in which a man's brow contracts. On this view the day is described by what occurs in it, as we said regarding "stern," since a day is not described as contracting what is between the eyes. Mujahid and Qatadah said: (p-435) "qamtarir" is that which contracts faces, draws in life, and what is between the eyes from its severity. al-Farra' said: it is severe.
